en: The Shorter Exposition:
The Exposition of the Chapter on the Way to the Far Shore;
The Exposition of the Questions.
2. The Exposition of the Young Brahmin Tissa Metteyya’s Question:
“Contented in the world with anger [as my wealth],” said the Venerable Tissa Metteyya.
For whom do no fluctuations exist?
Having directly known both extremes,
who, wise, is not stained by the middle?
Whom do you call a Great Man?
Who here has transcended the seamstress?
Who is at peace in the world? Who is content in the world, satisfied, joyful, and one whose purpose is fulfilled?
"Content with anger in the world.
Thus spoke the Venerable Tissa Metteyya.
"Thus" (*icca*) refers to the connection of words, the conjunction of words, the fulfillment of words, the combination of syllables, the smoothness of phonemes, and the sequential order of words.
"Thus. "Venerable" (*āyasmā*) is a term of endearment, a term of respect; it is a designation for one who possesses reverence and deference—this is what "venerable" means.
"Tissa" is the name, designation, concept, expression, appellation, naming, denomination, title, term, phrasing, and utterance of that brahmin.
"Metteyya" is the clan, designation, concept, expression, and appellation of that brahmin—
thus was the Venerable Tissa-Metteyya known.
“For whom do ‘shakings’ not exist?”—these are the shaking of craving, the shaking of views, the shaking of conceit, the shaking of defilements, and the shaking of sensual desire.

For whom these shakings are not present, do not exist, are not found, and are not obtained; for whom they have been abandoned, utterly cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt up by the fire of knowledge—for such a one, shakings do not exist.
"Who, having directly known both extremes": who, having directly known—that is, having understood, weighed, scrutinized, clarified, and made manifest—both extremes.

"The wise one is not smeared in the middle": the wise one is not smeared by means of wisdom; unsmeared, unbesmeared, gone out, escaped, utterly released, dissociated, he dwells with a mind for which the boundaries of the world no longer exist.
In the midst, the wise one is not defiled.
Whom do you call a "Great Man"? A Great Man, an eminent man, a superior man, a most excellent man, a preeminent man, a supreme man, a foremost man, a distinguished man.
Whom do you speak of? Whom do you describe? Whom do you conceive? Whom do you say? Whom do you perceive? Whom do you designate?
"Whom do you call a Great Man?

"Who here has transcended the seamstress? Who here has gone beyond, surpassed, overcome, and passed beyond the seamstress—that is, craving—who has transcended it?—this is "who here has transcended the seamstress."
Therefore that brahmin said:
“Content with anger in the world...
(Thus spoke the Venerable Tissa Metteyya.)
For whom do no stirrings exist?
Having directly known both ends, who,
wise, is not defiled in the middle?
"Whom do you call a Great Man?
Who here has transcended the seamstress?
"One who lives the holy life (brahmacariya) amidst sensual desires..."
"Metteyya," said the Blessed One,
"is a bhikkhu who is free from craving, ever mindful,
and having fully understood, has attained Nibbāna."
For him there are no fluctuations. "One who lives the holy life regarding sensual pleasures":
briefly, there are two kinds of sensual pleasures.
There are sensual pleasures as objects and sensual pleasures as defilements...
[as above] ...these are called sensual pleasures as objects...
[as above] ...these are called sensual pleasures as defilements.

"Brahmacariya" is said to be the refraining from, the abstaining from, the desisting from, the abstinence from, the non-doing, the non-performing, the non-transgression of, and the non-overstepping of the time-limit for engaging in unrighteous conduct (*asaddhamma*).
Furthermore, in its primary sense, "brahmacariya" refers to the Noble Eightfold Path, namely:
right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration.

One who is endowed with, fully endowed with, has approached, fully approached, has attained, fully attained, and is possessed of this noble eightfold path is called "one who lives the holy life" (*brahmacariyavā*).

And just as one is called "wealthy" because of wealth, "prosperous" because of prosperity, "famous" because of fame, "skilled" because of a craft, "virtuous" because of virtue, and "energetic" because of energy; so too is he called "one who lives the holy life."
Just as one who possesses wisdom is called "wise" and one who possesses true knowledge is called "possessing true knowledge," even so,

whoever is endowed with, fully endowed with, has approached, fully approached, has attained, fully attained, and is possessed of this Noble Eightfold Path, he is called "one who lives the holy life"— that is,
one who lives the holy life regarding sensual pleasures.
"Metteyya"—the Blessed One addresses that brahmin by his clan name.

"Blessed One" (Bhagavā) is a designation for one who is venerable... [as detailed in the standard formula] ...it is a descriptive term based on realization, namely "Blessed One"—thus says the Blessed One: "Metteyya."
"Free from craving, ever mindful.
Craving (*taṇhā*) refers to craving for forms … [and so on] … craving for mental phenomena (*dhamma*).
For one by whom this craving has been abandoned, utterly cut off, stilled, subsided, and rendered incapable of arising through the fire of knowledge—
Burnt up, he is said to be one whose craving is gone, whose craving is abandoned, whose craving is vomited out, whose craving is released, whose craving is relinquished, whose craving is renounced;
one who is free from passion, whose passion is gone, whose passion is abandoned, whose passion is released, whose passion is relinquished, whose passion is renounced;
one who is hungerless, extinguished, become cool, experiencing bliss, and dwelling with self become as Brahmā.

Always, ever, at all times, at every time, constantly, perpetually, continuously, uninterruptedly, in immediate succession, like the falling of raindrops, without interval, in a continuous stream, joined together, in contact—before the meal, after the meal, during the first watch, the middle watch, and the last watch;
in the dark fortnight, the bright fortnight; in the rainy season, the winter, and the summer; in the first stage of life, the middle stage, and so forth.
In the final aggregate of life, in the final aggregate of life.
"Mindful" means mindful by way of four reasons:
being mindful while developing the foundation of mindfulness through contemplation of the body as body.

One who, being mindful, develops the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating feelings in feelings; being mindful, develops the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating the mind in the mind; being mindful, develops the foundation of mindfulness by contemplating phenomena in phenomena … [as before] … he is called “mindful”—one who is always mindful, free from craving.
"A bhikkhu who has attained Nibbāna through discernment": here "discernment" (saṅkhā) is said to mean knowledge.
It is wisdom, understanding, investigation, thorough investigation... non-delusion, the investigation of phenomena, right view.

"Through discernment" means having discerned, known, weighed, judged, clarified, and made manifest; that is, having discerned, known, weighed, judged, clarified, and made manifest that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent."

“Having reckoned, known, weighed, scrutinized, and made manifest [the fact] that ‘all conditioned phenomena are suffering’; … ‘all phenomena are non-self’; … ‘with ignorance as condition there are volitional formations’;

… and so on … ‘whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation’—having reckoned them as impermanent, having known them, weighed them, scrutinized them, scrutinized them thoroughly, and made them manifest;

or alternatively, having reckoned them as suffering, as a disease, as a tumor, as a dart, … and so on … having reckoned them as an escape, having known them, weighed them, scrutinized them, scrutinized them thoroughly, and made them manifest.”
“Extinguished” means: extinguished because lust has been extinguished; extinguished because hatred has been extinguished; extinguished because delusion has been extinguished;
[extinguished] because anger… resentment… contempt… domineering… envy… avarice… deceit… fraud… obstinacy… aggression… conceit… arrogance… and intoxication have been extinguished.
... because of the extinguishing of negligence ... of all defilements ... of all misconduct ... of all distresses ...
of all fevers ... of all torments ... of all unwholesome volitional formations, he is "extinguished" (nibbuto).
He is a "bhikkhu" because of the breaking (*bhinna*) of seven things ... [as before] ... having lived the life, with renewed existence exhausted—he is a bhikkhu.
"The bhikkhu, having fully understood, is extinguished;
for him there are no more stirrings.
"For him" refers to the Arahant whose taints are destroyed.
"Quiverings" means the quivering of craving, the quivering of views, the quivering of conceit, the quivering of defilements, and the quivering of sensual desire.

These quiverings do not exist for him; they are not present, are not found, and are not apprehended. They have been abandoned, cut off, stilled, and subsided; they are incapable of arising again, being burnt up by the fire of knowledge—thus, "for him there are no quiverings."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Living the holy life regarding sensual pleasures,” (said the Blessed One, “Metteyya”).
Free from craving, always mindful,
having fully understood and attained Nibbāna—
the monk for whom there are no more stirrings.
Thus, having directly known both ends,
the wise one is not defiled by the middle;
him I call a Great Man.
Thus here he has transcended the seamstress.
Having directly known both ends, the wise one is not smeared in the middle.
"Ends": contact is one end, the arising of contact is the second end, and the cessation of contact is the middle.
The past is one extreme, the future is the second extreme, and the present is the middle.
Pleasant feeling is one extreme, painful feeling is the second extreme, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is the middle.
Name is one extreme, form is the second extreme, and consciousness is the middle.
The six internal sense bases are one extreme; the six external sense bases are the second extreme; consciousness is in between. Personality is one extreme;
the origin of personality is the second extreme; the cessation of personality is in between.
"Wisdom" is said to be discernment—that which is discernment, understanding... non-delusion, investigation of phenomena, right view.
There are two kinds of clinging:
the clinging of craving and the clinging of views.
What is the clinging of craving?
To whatever extent there is that which is delimited, encompassed, bounded, appropriated, and claimed as "mine" by way of craving—
thinking, "This is mine, this belongs to me, this much is mine, to this extent I have forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, rugs, coverlets,
female and male slaves, goats and sheep, chickens and pigs, elephants, cattle, horses and mares, fields and lands"— that is the limit.
“Gold and bullion, villages, market towns, royal capitals, kingdoms, and provinces, as well as treasuries and storehouses.
He even regards the entire great earth as his own through the power of craving.
To the extent that there are the eight hundred modes of the wandering of craving—
This is the smear of craving.
What is the smear of views?
The twenty-based view of a personal body (sakkāyadiṭṭhi), the ten-based wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi), and the ten-based view of grasping at extremes (antaggāhikā diṭṭhi).
View: such a view as this—a state of view, a thicket of view, a wilderness of view, a distortion of view, a vacillation of view, a fetter of view;
a grasping, a seizing, an adherence, an insistence, a wrong path, a false course, a state of error, a sectarian standpoint, a perverted grasp, a distorted grasp, a subverted grasp, a false grasp.
The grasping at what is not as it really is as being as it really is—namely, the sixty-two views—this is the "stain of views.
"Having directly known both ends, the wise one is not smeared in the middle": by means of wisdom, he [understands] both ends and the middle.
Having known through direct knowledge, having understood, weighed, scrutinized, and fully clarified it, one is not smeared, not defiled, not stained;
unsmeared, undefiled, unstained, gone forth, escaped, liberated, and dissociated,
one dwells with a mind that has transcended all boundaries.
Having directly known both ends, the wise one is not defiled by the middle.
Him I call a "great person"—a great person, a foremost person, a best person, a most excellent person, a preeminent person, a supreme person, a distinguished person, a sublime person.
Of him I speak, of him I talk, of him I declare, of him I illuminate, of him I discourse.
The Venerable Sāriputta said this to the Blessed One:
“Venerable sir, it is said, ‘a great man, a great man.
In what way, venerable sir, is one a great man?”
“Sāriputta, it is because his mind is liberated that I call one a ‘great man’; I do not call one a ‘great man’ because his mind is not liberated.
And how, Sāriputta, is the mind liberated?
Here, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.”
As he dwells contemplating the body in the body, his mind becomes dispassionate and is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
[The same applies to] feelings … pe … the mind …
He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world.
As he dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, his mind becomes dispassionate and is liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
In this way, Sāriputta, a bhikkhu is one whose mind is liberated.

“Sāriputta, it is because of having a liberated mind that I call one a ‘Great Man’; it is because of not having a liberated mind that I do not call one a ‘Great Man. Therefore, I say he is a Great Man.
He has here transcended the seamstress: by ‘seamstress’ is meant craving.”

Whatever lust, infatuation, ... [as above] ... covetousness, greed, the root of unwholesomeness—for whomsoever this needle of craving has been abandoned, cut off, stilled, subsided, rendered incapable of arising, and burnt away by the fire of knowledge—he has gone beyond, transcended, surpassed, overcome, and passed over that needle of craving;
thus it is said: "He here has gone beyond the needle."
Therefore the Blessed One said:
“Having directly known both extremes,
the wise one is not defiled in the middle.”
“Him I call a Great Man;
he has here transcended the seamstress.

At the conclusion of this verse, for those thousands of beings who shared the same aspiration, the same application, the same purpose, and were imbued with the same latent tendencies as the brahmin, the dustless, stainless Eye of Dhamma arose.
“Whatever is subject to arising, all that is subject to cessation.
With this, the brahmin’s mind was liberated from the taints through non-clinging.
Simultaneously with his attainment of arahantship, his deerskin, matted hair, bark garments, triple staff, water-pot, head hair, and beard disappeared.
Clad in garments dyed with *bhaṇḍuka* dye, wearing his outer robe, bowl, and robes, he sat with palms joined in homage to the Blessed One, practicing in accordance with the purpose:
"Venerable sir, the Blessed One is my teacher; I am a disciple.
This concludes the second exposition: The Questions of the Young Man Tissa Metteyya.
